solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Suddenly attack American submarine around the opening of Hormuz (6)

indicatorNotes.around: turned around, so SUB reads backwards
indicatorNotes.the opening of: the opening of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: SUB, short for submarine, turned around

annotation.surface: A news report of a US submarine launching a surprise strike at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz.
annotation.walkthrough: The naval setting makes 'around' look like the sub circling the strait; it only asks you to turn SUB round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb means to spring out on someone from hiding, the whole point being surprise.

entries.clue: Three articles eviscerating Madonna? That’s an abomination! (8)

indicatorNotes.eviscerating: gutting Madonna removes her insides, leaving only the outer letters

blocks.note: the articles AN, A and THE
MADONNA with its insides removed leaves M…A

annotation.surface: An outraged critic reviewing magazine pieces that tear the pop star Madonna apart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Articles' reads as newspaper pieces savaging the singer; in grammar the articles are A, AN and THE.
annotation.definitionFit: Originally a church curse, the word now names anything loathed, so 'an abomination' is a plain synonym.

entries.clue: Rotten time to engage in playful talk (8)

indicatorNotes.to engage: to engage is to hold or take in, as one gear engages another, so the outer word takes the smaller one inside

blocks.note: an age = a period of time

annotation.surface: Someone grumbling that it is a bad moment to start bantering.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Engage in' reads as one phrasal verb; split it, and 'in' becomes the very letters that get engaged.
annotation.definitionFit: Badinage is light, teasing, playful conversation.

entries.clue: Diminished newspaper relying on Kelvin? (4)

blocks.note: K = kelvin, the unit of temperature

annotation.surface: A shrunken newspaper leaning on someone called Kelvin to keep it afloat.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue SUN sits on top of K, so 'relying on' describes the stacking. The Sun is a British daily tabloid.
annotation.definitionFit: Something sunk has gone down, fallen to a lower level, diminished.

entries.clue: Expert/ace crew member catching flatfish (1,3,4)

indicatorNotes.catching: to catch something is to hold it, so the outer letters close around the fish

blocks.note: A = ace, as on playing cards
a dab is a small flatfish
a hand is a member of a ship's crew

annotation.surface: A skilled deckhand on a fishing boat hauling in a flatfish.
annotation.walkthrough: The slash shows 'Expert' and 'ace' are two separate words, not one phrase; only 'Expert' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A British informal idiom for someone very skilled at something, as in being handy in the kitchen.

entries.clue: Store license’s date ran out (12)

indicatorNotes.ran out: the letters run off in disorder

annotation.surface: A shopkeeper worried because their trading licence has expired.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored, so the S counts as a letter of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A delicatessen is a shop selling prepared foods.

entries.clue: Blair urges reforms to petty crimes (10)

indicatorNotes.reforms to: the letters are re-formed into something new

annotation.surface: Tony Blair, the former British prime minister, calling for changes to the law on minor offences.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reforms' fits a politician so well it reads as policy; here it turns the letters over.
annotation.definitionFit: Burglaries are break-in thefts, crimes against property.

entries.clue: Acknowledge Laycock regularly noted record temperature (6)

indicatorNotes.regularly: take letters at regular intervals: lAyCoCk

blocks.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of LAYCOCK

annotation.surface: Admitting that a man called Laycock routinely logged a record high temperature.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Record temperature' wants to be a heatwave headline; it splits into EP and T.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean admitting that something is so, as when you concede a point.

entries.clue: Sweet song Leonard Cohen initially penned (6)

indicatorNotes.initially: 'initially' means at the start, so each name gives only its opening letter
indicatorNotes.penned: a pen is also an enclosure, so what is penned is shut inside another word

blocks.note: a duet is a song for two
first letters of Leonard and Cohen

annotation.surface: Praise for a lovely song that Leonard Cohen wrote early in his career.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Penned' is exactly what a songwriter does, so it reads as authorship; here it means enclosed.
annotation.definitionFit: Dulcet means sweet and soothing, usually of sound.

entries.clue: Burning area of forest close to Stockport (6)

indicatorNotes.close to: the close of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: the Forest of Arden, in Warwickshire, England

annotation.surface: A report of a woodland fire near Stockport, a town in Greater Manchester.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as 'near' Stockport; it means the town's final letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Ardent literally means burning, and figuratively passionate.

entries.clue: Start to clean large, lacier pants belonging to the vicar? (8)

indicatorNotes.Start to: the start of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.pants: British slang for rubbish, so the letters are messed up

blocks.note: L = large, as on clothing sizes

annotation.surface: Someone about to launder a pair of rather lacy underpants that turn out to be the vicar's.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like underwear; as a verb-like indicator it is British slang for bad, shaking up LACIER.
annotation.definitionFit: Clerical means relating to the clergy, such as a vicar.

entries.clue: One used to hear a call for order? (12)

annotation.definition: One used to hear a call for order?

blocks.note: reads as the Speaker of the House of Commons shouting 'Order!' to calm MPs
really a telephone call you listen to through a loudspeaker, hands free

annotation.surface: A riddle about the device, or person, you hear a demand for order through.
annotation.walkthrough: A speakerphone lets you hear a phone call; 'call for order' also suggests the Speaker of the House of Commons calling 'Order!'.
annotation.definitionFit: A speakerphone is a telephone you hear a call on without holding it.

entries.clue: Sharpen new garden tool outside (4)

indicatorNotes.outside: one word placed outside another wraps round it, so the tool surrounds the single letter

blocks.note: a hoe is a weeding tool

annotation.surface: A gardener sharpening a new tool out in the garden.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outside' sits naturally with gardening, suggesting outdoors; it places HOE around N.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the hone, a whetstone used to put an edge on blades.

entries.clue: A Pepsi cola one’s left for Yankee ordered in The World’s End (10)

indicatorNotes.left for: the I leaves and Y takes its place
indicatorNotes.ordered in: the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: I (one) goes, replaced by Y (Yankee in the NATO alphabet)

annotation.surface: Someone ordering a Pepsi in The World's End, a pub name, with an American in the bar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The World's End' is a common English pub name, so 'ordered in' reads as buying a drink there.
annotation.definitionFit: The biblical Revelation's vision of final destruction, so 'The World's End' fits, capital letters and all.

entries.clue: Baroque composer taking time out over new advanced infection (10)

indicatorNotes.out: 'taking out' is removing, as a dentist takes a tooth out, so one letter goes
indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, SCARLATI sits over the rest

blocks.note: A = advanced, as in A level

annotation.surface: A Baroque composer taking time off with a new illness at an advanced stage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taking time out' reads as a rest; T is time, and only one of the composer's two Ts leaves.
annotation.definitionFit: Scarlatina is another name for scarlet fever, an infection.

entries.clue: Mum, Joe and family rent refurbished projector (5,7)

indicatorNotes.refurbished: RENT is done up into a new form

blocks.note: a clan is an extended family

annotation.surface: A family renting out a newly renovated home, with Mum and Joe in charge.
annotation.walkthrough: Joe is a plain first name in the surface; it becomes GI via GI Joe, the US soldier.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by type: the Victorian device threw painted glass slides onto a screen, an early projector.

entries.clue: Empty flipping hollow before you had dinner? (8)

annotation.surface: An exasperated host asking whether you ate before arriving and left the plate empty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word, and 'Empty' as an adjective; it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: clearing out a building, or the bowels, is emptying it.

entries.clue: Sign of star broadcaster is khaki trousers (8)

indicatorNotes.trousers: as a verb, to trouser is to pocket, so the phrase holds the answer

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word across 'is' into the start of the third

annotation.surface: A star presenter recognised by their khaki trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' reads as clothing; used as a verb it means pockets, and the phrase before it pockets the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: The asterisk is the little star-shaped sign in print.

entries.clue: Folk song’s eco-friendly record covers (12)

blocks.note: record sleeves are the covers of vinyl albums

annotation.surface: A folk song released on vinyl in recycled sleeves.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Tudor ballad, legendarily by Henry VIII, is England's best-known folk tune.

entries.clue: Privy near bottom of street (6)

indicatorNotes.bottom of: in a down clue the bottom of a word is its last letter

annotation.surface: Directions to a toilet at the far end of the street.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Privy' looks like the noun for an outdoor toilet; as an adjective it means secret, like closet.
annotation.definitionFit: Privy and closet both mean secret or private, as in a closet admirer.

entries.clue: Show Gene Vincent hosts (6)

indicatorNotes.hosts: the phrase hosts the answer inside it

blocks.note: the last letter of the first name runs on into the first five of the surname

annotation.surface: Gene Vincent, the 1950s rock and roll singer, presenting a TV show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Show' and 'hosts' look like television; show is the verb here.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain, rather formal synonym: you reveal or display a quality, as in evincing surprise.

entries.clue: Slav people produced veg (4,6)

indicatorNotes.produced: the letters are made into something new

annotation.surface: A Slavic community growing its own vegetables.
annotation.walkthrough: Love apple is an old name for the tomato.
annotation.definitionFit: Love apples are tomatoes, eaten as vegetables.

entries.clue: Top Conservative featured in naked cameo (4)

indicatorNotes.featured in: C features inside the stripped word
indicatorNotes.naked: CAMEO stripped of its outer letters

blocks.note: CAMEO without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A leading Tory politician appearing in a brief nude film role.
annotation.walkthrough: C goes after the A of AME, making A-C-ME.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the Greek for a point: the peak or height of something.

entries.clue: Silly idea periodically supported by this paper (4)

indicatorNotes.supported by: in a down clue DA sits on top of FT

blocks.note: second and fourth letters of IDEA
the Financial Times, where this crossword appeared

annotation.surface: A daft idea that this newspaper nonetheless backs every so often.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This paper' is the setter's own newspaper, the FT.
annotation.definitionFit: A British informal synonym for foolish, as in 'don't be daft'.

entries.clue: The club I go to when I’m splashing out? (4,4)

annotation.definition: The club I go to when I’m splashing out?

blocks.note: reads as a nightclub or members' club; really a golf club
reads as spending lavishly; really blasting the ball out of a bunker in a spray of sand

annotation.surface: Someone naming the nightclub they head for when spending freely.
annotation.walkthrough: A golfer in a bunker splashes the ball out with sand; 'club' and 'splashing out' pretend to mean a nightspot and a spree.
annotation.definitionFit: A sand iron is a golf club, the sand wedge, for playing out of bunkers.

entries.clue: Son returns service in first-class big game experience (6)

indicatorNotes.returns: to return is to go back the way you came, so the word is read backwards
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts one thing inside another, so the reversed service sits within first-class

blocks.note: A1 = first-class, written with I for 1
the Royal Air Force, one of the armed services

annotation.surface: A son coming back to serve in a top-flight match.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Returns service' and 'big game' read as tennis; 'service' is the RAF, and 'big game' means wild animals.
annotation.definitionFit: A safari is an expedition to see or hunt big game.

entries.clue: Youngster ate green bananas (8)

indicatorNotes.bananas: slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

annotation.surface: A child eating unripe bananas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Green bananas' reads as unripe fruit; 'green' is fodder and 'bananas' means crazy.
annotation.definitionFit: A teenager is a youngster aged thirteen to nineteen.

entries.clue: Karts wheeling round Silverstone at the back barely run (6)

indicatorNotes.wheeling: wheeling is turning and circling, so the letters spin into a new order
indicatorNotes.round: the rearranged KARTS go round E
indicatorNotes.at the back: the back of a word is its last letter

annotation.surface: Go-karts circling Silverstone, the British Grand Prix circuit, only just finishing a run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Barely run' reads as a narrow finish for the karts; 'barely' actually means without clothes.
annotation.definitionFit: To streak is to run naked in public, as at sports events.
